I.	People came to him when the patient was on his last legs. Dr. Raman often burst out, ‘Why
couldn’t you have come a day earlier? The reason was obvious—visiting fee twenty-five rupees,
and more than that, people liked to shirk the fact that the time had come to call in Dr. Raman; for
them there was something ominous in the very association. As a result, when the big man came on
the scene it was always a quick decision one way or another. There was no scope or time for any
kind of wavering or whitewashing. Long years of practice of this kind had bred in the doctor a
certain curt truthfulness; for that very reason his opinion was valued; he was not a mere doctor
expressing an opinion but a judge pronouncing a verdict. The patient’s life hung on his words. This
never unduly worried Dr. Raman. He never believed that agreeable words ever saved lives. He did
not think it was any of his business to provide comforting lies when as a matter of course nature
would tell them the truth in a few hours. However, when he glimpsed the faintest sign of hope, he
rolled up his sleeve and stepped into the arena: it might be hours or days, but he never withdrew
till he wrested the prize from Yama’s hands.
Source: Extract and edits from The Doctor’s World by R. K. Narayan

II.	The Peshawar and Sholapur episodes during the Civil Disobedience Movement of 1930 revealed
the shifting nature of British colonial authority and the growing fearlessness of the Indian masses.
In Peshawar, the atmosphere became electric when the arrest of local leaders led to a massive
upsurge. Here, a significant event occurred that shook the very foundations of the British Raj: the
refusal of the Garhwali soldiers to fire on their unarmed Muslim compatriots. This instance of
cross-communal and cross-class solidarity among the armed forces indicated that the traditional
instruments of colonial repression were no longer entirely reliable.
Simultaneously, in the industrial town of Sholapur, the movement took a more radical turn.
Following the news of Gandhiji’s arrest, textile workers went on a strike that transformed into a
virtual takeover of the town. For several days, British administration effectively vanished, and the
rebels established a parallel government. This was not merely a protest; it was a demonstration of
the "power of the street" where laborers, often viewed as politically inert, became the vanguard of
the nationalist struggle.
The movement’s strength lay in its unprecedented mobilization of women. For the first time,
women from various socio-economic backgrounds—from affluent urban households to rural
peasant families—marched in processions, picketed liquor shops, and faced lathi charges with
stoic endurance. This shattered the domestic-public divide that had characterized earlier political
phases. Furthermore, the commercial classes, hit hard by the Great Depression, threw their
financial weight behind the Congress, seeing in Swaraj a shield against discriminatory colonial
economic policies.
However, unlike the Non-Cooperation era, communal unity remained fragile. While certain
pockets saw joint participation, the formal distancing of large sections of the Muslim political
leadership created a vacuum that would later be filled by separatist ideologies. Despite this, the
movement proved that Indian nationalism had matured into a sophisticated, multi-layered force
capable of paralyzing the colonial state through disciplined non-violence.
Source: Extracted, with edits and revisions, from India After Gandhi and History of Modern India,
by Ramachandra Guha and Bipin Chandra.

questions.stimulus:
Ill. The optimism surrounding the "Third Wave" of democratization was largely predicated on the
belief that information technology would act as an irreversible catalyst for liberty. In the early
2000s, it was argued that the decentralized nature of the internet would make it impossible for
autocratic regimes to control the flow of information. However, the subsequent decade witnessed
the rise of "digital authoritarianism," a sophisticated model where state actors utilize data and
technology to entrench their power rather than relinquish it. This shift has fundamentally altered
the global political landscape, creating what some scholars call a "technological iron curtain."

Central to this transformation is the weaponization of social media and the deployment of
advanced surveillance systems. Unlike the overt repression of the twentieth century, modern
illiberal regimes often employ "informational autocracy," where they manipulate public opinion
through state-sponsored disinformation and algorithmic censorship. This allows the state to
maintain a facade of democratic legitimacy while systematically hollowing out the institutions
that protect civil liberties. Furthermore, the export of surveillance technology from dominant
autocratic powers to developing nations has facilitated a "normative shift," making high-tech
monitoring a standardized tool of governance. www.lawpreptutorial.com
By 2020, the retreat from democratic norms had reached a critical juncture. The promise that
prosperity and global connectivity would naturally lead to liberal outcomes was challenged by the
resilience of state-led capitalism. Freedom House reported that the gap between democratic gains
and losses had widened for the fifteenth consecutive year. The "democratic recession" identified
earlier in the century had evolved into a more profound "democratic depression," characterized by
the erosion of judicial independence and the suppression of independent media in even established
democracies.

Zuboff and The Road to Unfreedom by Timothy Snyder.

questions.stimulus:
IV.	American literature represents a distinct and vigorous tradition that has profoundly shaped the
global literary landscape. From the brooding transcendentalism of Ralph Waldo Emerson to the
gritty realism of Mark Twain and the innovative modernism of F. Scott Fitzgerald, it offers a
diverse exploration of the "American Dream" and its inherent contradictions. A foundational figure
is Nathaniel Hawthorne, whose masterpiece The Scarlet Letter remains a seminal study of guilt,
sin, and the rigid morality of Puritan New England. His exploration of the "dark side" of the
human psyche paved the way for the American Gothic tradition.
The mid-19th century witnessed a "literary renaissance" fueled by the transcendentalist
movement. Henry David Thoreau’s Walden advocated for simple living and a deep, spiritual
connection to nature, while Walt Whitman’s Leaves of Grass broke traditional poetic forms with
its expansive free verse, celebrating democracy and the individual. Later, Mark Twain introduced
a new vernacular realism in Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, using humor and regional dialect to
provide a scathing critique of slavery and social hypocrisy. His work signaled a shift away from
European literary models toward a uniquely American voice.
In the 20th century, the "Lost Generation" emerged, disillusioned by the aftermath of World War
I. F. Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby remains the definitive critique of the Jazz Age, capturing
the glitter and hollowness of obsession. Simultaneously, the Harlem Renaissance brought Black
intellectual and artistic life to the forefront; Langston Hughes used the rhythms of jazz and blues
in his poetry to explore the African American experience. Post-war literature saw further
diversification, with Toni Morrison’s Beloved utilizing magical realism to address the harrowing
legacy of slavery.
Today, American literature continues to reflect a multicultural society. Authors like Jhumpa
Lahiri, in The Namesake, explore themes of diaspora, identity, and the immigrant experience.
Ultimately, American literature is a dynamic mirror of a nation in constant flux, utilizing a vast
array of styles to interrogate the complexities of freedom, heritage, and the human condition.
Source: Adapted and revised from The Norton Anthology of American Literature and A Brief
History of American Literature by Richard Gray.

replaces the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (MGNREGA), which
was enacted during the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance government and had been in
force for nearly two decades.
According to the Centre, the VB-G Ram G Act introduces significant structural changes while
expanding the legal guarantee of employment in rural areas. One of the key changes is the
increase in the number of guaranteed days of work per household from 100 to 125 days. The
government has positioned this as a step toward strengthening livelihood security for rural
families and improving the quality and impact of public works undertaken under the scheme.
The legislation has, however, drawn criticism from opposition parties and some civil society
groups. Responding to these concerns, Union Minister for wooe---(2)------- Shivraj Singh Chouhan
released a video message defending the new Act. He accused critics of attempting to “mislead” the
public and create “confusion” by portraying the law as a dilution of MGNREGA. Emphasising
continuity rather than dismantling, Mr. Chouhan said the VB-G Ram G Act builds upon and
improves the earlier framework.
Describing the new scheme as “a step forward from MGNREGA,” the Minister highlighted that
provisions related to unemployment allowance have been strengthened. He also pointed out that
the law includes penalties for delays in wage payments, an issue that has frequently affected
workers under the earlier scheme. To support the expanded and restructured programme, the
government has earmarked a budget of 21,51,282 crore, which it says will be used for the
comprehensive development of villages across the country.

primarily focused on the creation of “works,” the VB-G Ram G aims to generate measurable
“outcomes.” Under the new framework, projects will be concentrated in four key areas: water
security, core rural infrastructure, livelihood-related infrastructure, and mitigation of the impacts
of extreme weather events. The Centre will continue as the principal funding partner, following
the 60:40 cost-sharing model used in most centrally sponsored schemes.

officially launched on Sunday, with ground-level surveys having already begun last month. Union
Environment Minister Bhupender Yadav chaired a high-level joint meeting of the National Tiger
Conservation Authority (NTCA) and the Project Elephant Steering Committee at the Sundarbans
Tiger Reserve. He emphasized that India’s conservation model must increasingly be science-driven
and supported by international collaboration, citing recent delegations from South Africa,
Namibia, and Botswana associated with the cheetah reintroduction programme.
Addressing the growing issue of human—wildlife conflict, Yadav outlined a three-pronged strategy
and announced a specialised initiative titled “Management of Tigers Outside Tiger Reserves.”
Officials also highlighted persistent challenges such as staff shortages, financial limitations, and
the urgent need to control invasive species that threaten wildlife habitats.
On elephant conservation, the Steering Committee reviewed progress on the All-India
Synchronized Elephant Estimation and DNA profiling of captive elephants. Particular focus was
placed on the Nilgiri Elephant Reserve and the Ripu—Chirang Elephant Reserve, along with
renewed attention on assessing elephant corridors and conflict-prone areas in the Bandhavgarh
region. www.lawpreptutorial.com
Following the meeting, Yadav addressed the media on the recent deaths of elephants in a train
collision in Assam’s Hojai district, where seven elephants were killed after being hit by the
Sairang—New Delhi Rajdhani Express, and a calf later died from injuries. The Centre has sought a
detailed report on the incident, and railway authorities have been directed to coordinate closely
with state forest departments to monitor elephant movement along railway tracks. The minister
noted that 1,100 elephant accident-prone zones have been identified across the country, and
district magistrates have been instructed to keep forest officials informed about elephant
movement along highways.
Yadav also disclosed that %112 crore for tiger conservation and %344 crore for elephant-related
projects have been allocated to the Sundarbans over the past five years, though a significant
portion remains unutilised. He compared tourism figures, noting that while the Sundarbans

attract around 9.5 lakh visitors annually, Ranthambore generates 718-19 lakh, stressing the need
for better promotion while maintaining ecological balance.
The meeting ratified several NTCA technical committee decisions, including approval of tiger
conservation plans, expansion of Project Cheetah, tiger translocation, prey-base augmentation,
landscape planning, carnivore health training, and inputs to the National Board for Wildlife.
Updates were shared on expanding Project Cheetah to Gandhisagar Wildlife Sanctuary and
Gujarat’s Banni Grassland. Preparations for a proposed Global Big Cat Summit were reviewed,
and six key publications were released, reinforcing the government’s commitment to a community-
centric conservation approach.

VII. Over the past decade, China and India have shown sharply divergent trajectories in tackling air
pollution. Once infamous for its smog, Beijing reduced its annual PM2.5 levels by more than 50%
between 2013 and 2021, whereas Delhi continues to rank among the world’s most polluted cities.
Beijing’s clean-air transformation resulted from a multifaceted, top-down approach anchored in
coherent policy, strict enforcement, and regional coordination. Key interventions included the Air
Pollution Prevention and Control Action Plan and the Blue Sky Protection Campaign, which
targeted energy, transport, and industry. The government expanded electric mobility, shut down
or relocated polluting industries, replaced coal-fired boilers with natural gas, imposed China VI
vehicular emission standards, and built a dense PM2.5 real-time monitoring system with
substantial penalties for non-compliance. Coordination with neighbouring Tianjin-Hebei provinces
through a unified ‘airshed’ strategy ensured that transboundary pollution was effectively
regulated. These measures drove PM2.5 levels down from 102 pg/m* in 2013 to 31 pg/m* in 2024.
India, by contrast, has a strong statutory framework for environmental protection, including the
Air (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1981, the Environment Protection Act, 1986, and
rules covering waste, construction, and emissions. Initiatives such as the National Clean Air
Programme, Graded Response Action Plan, odd-even vehicle rationing, and the Commission for
Air Quality Management (CAQM) exist, yet they are largely reactive and fragmented. Multiple
agencies—from the Union government to municipal bodies—function in silos, slowing decision-
making, weakening enforcement, and diffusing accountability. Pollution control boards are
chronically underfunded and understaffed, and regional coordination, particularly to tackle
stubble burning, remains ineffective.
China’s success also stems from sustained investment in clean energy, electric mobility, and
industrial relocation, whereas Delhi’s attempts, such as the Bawana project and waste-to-energy
plants, have faltered. Delhi’s pollution is compounded by industrial and vehicular emissions,
construction dust, open waste burning, and meteorological inversions. Public transport expansion
and behavioral change have lagged, and temporary measures like odd-even rationing have limited
long-term impact.
For India to achieve meaningful improvement, it need not replicate China’s political system but
can adopt key principles: long-term, mission-oriented governance treating air pollution as a public
health emergency; accelerated clean-energy transition; enforceable transport reforms including
BS-VI compliance, EV infrastructure, and public transport expansion; functional industrial
relocation with monitoring; and regional coordination akin to Beijing’s airshed model for the
Delhi-NCR region.
Source — The Hindu article dated 224 December, 2025

water resource projects of India covering four states—Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and
Rajasthan. The Sardar Sarovar project would meet the requirement of water in drought-prone and
desert areas. Sardar Sarovar Project will provide irrigation facilities to 18.45 lakh hectare of land,
covering 3112 villages in 15 districts of Gujarat. It will also irrigate 2,46,000 hectare of land in the
strategic desert districts of Barmer and Jalore in Rajasthan and 37,500 hectare in the tribal hilly
tract of Maharashtra through lift. About 75 per cent of the command area in Gujarat is drought
prone while entire command in Rajasthan is drought prone. Assured water supply will soon make
this area drought proof.
However, in recent years, multi-purpose projects and large dams have come under great scrutiny
and opposition for a variety of reasons. Regulating and damming of rivers affect their natural flow
causing poor sediment flow and excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir, resulting
in rockier stream beds and poorer habitats for the rivers’ aquatic life. Dams also fragment rivers
making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially for spawning. The reservoirs that are
created on the floodplains also submerge the existing vegetation and soil leading to its
decomposition over a period of time.www.lawpreptutorial.com
These floods have not only devastated life and property but also caused extensive soil erosion.
Sedimentation also meant that the flood plains were deprived of silt, a natural fertiliser, further
adding on to the problem of land degradation. It was also observed that the multi purpose projects
induced earthquakes, caused water-borne diseases and pests and pollution resulting from

excessive use of water. Irrigation has also changed the cropping pattern of many regions with
farmers shifting to water intensive and commercial crops. This has great ecological consequences
like salinisation of the soil. Pradhan Mantri Krishi Sinchayee Yojana has been started which
ensures access to some means to protective irrigation for all agricultural farms in the country,
thus bringing much desired rural prosperity. Some of the broad objectives of this programme are
to enhance the physical access of water on the farm and expand cultivable area under assured
irrigation (har khet ko pani), improve on-farm water use efficiency to reduce wastage and increase
availability both in duration and extent, irrigation and other water saving technologies (per drop
more crop) and introduce sustainable water conservation practices, etc.

questions.stimulus:
IX.	The concept of power-sharing has developed as a response to the earlier belief in the concentration
of political power in the hands of a single person or group. Traditionally, it was assumed that
centralized power allowed governments to take quick decisions and enforce them effectively.
Distributing power, it was feared, would weaken authority and slow down governance. However,
with the rise of democratic systems, these ideas have changed significantly. Democracy rests on
the principle that all political power originates from the people. In a democratic setup, citizens
govern themselves through institutions of self-government, and due respect is given to the
diversity of opinions, interests, and social groups present in society. To ensure meaningful
participation and representation, political power must be shared among a wide section of the
population.
Modern democracies adopt various power-sharing arrangements. One important form is the
horizontal distribution of power among the three main organs of government: the legislature,
executive, and judiciary. Although these institutions operate at the same level, they are assigned
different responsibilities and powers. This separation ensures that no single organ can dominate
the others or misuse authority. Each institution acts as a check on the powers of the others,
creating a balance known as the system of checks and balances. For instance, the executive is
accountable to the legislature, while the judiciary can review the actions of both the legislature
and the executive to ensure they follow constitutional principles.
Another significant form of power-sharing is vertical distribution, where authority is divided
among different levels of government. This includes a central or federal government for the entire
country and state or regional governments for different provinces. In India, this system exists
between the Union Government and the State Governments, with the Constitution clearly
defining their respective powers. This principle is also extended to local levels of governance such
as municipalities and panchayats, allowing citizens to participate directly in decision-making at
the grassroots level.
Power can also be shared among different social groups, including religious, linguistic, and ethnic
communities. Such arrangements help ensure fair representation of minorities and socially
weaker sections in governance. Examples include Belgium’s community government and India’s
system of reserved constituencies, which aim to prevent marginalization and foster social
harmony.
Lastly, power-sharing occurs through political parties, pressure groups, and social movements.
Competition among political parties ensures that power does not remain concentrated in one hand.
Coalition governments, formed by alliances of parties, are a direct example of shared power.
Additionally, interest groups influence policymaking by representing various sections of society,
thereby strengthening democratic participation and accountability.
(Source - NCERT Class X, Democratic Politics)

questions.stimulus:
XI.	Judicial review signifies the supremacy of law and embodies the authority of courts to examine the
actions of the Legislature, the Executive, and even the Judiciary itself, in order to assess their
conformity with the Constitution. It empowers constitutional courts to scrutinize the validity of
laws, policies, and governmental actions, ensuring that they remain within the bounds prescribed
by the supreme law of the land. Over time, judicial review has evolved into one of the most potent
mechanisms for safeguarding individual liberties in a constitutional democracy and for reinforcing
foundational principles such as the rule of law and the separation of powers. By exercising this
power, the Judiciary acts as a constitutional sentinel, preventing the decisions and actions of other
branches of government from undermining or violating constitutional values. The Constitution, by
its very nature, functions as a document of limitation. Rather than conferring unchecked
authority, it restrains the exercise of power by the State and protects society from the excesses of
majoritarian rule. In this framework, judicial review operates as a protective shield placed in the
hands of constitutional courts, enabling them to preserve the supremacy of the Constitution and to
ensure that democratic governance does not degenerate into arbitrary or unconstitutional exercise
of power. Through this mechanism, courts uphold the delicate balance among the three branches
of government while ensuring that constitutional guarantees remain meaningful and effective.
The scope and contours of judicial review, particularly in relation to legislative enactments, were
elaborated by the Supreme Court in Binoy Viswam v. Union of India & Ors. The Court clarified
that under the Constitution of India, both the Supreme Court and the High Courts are vested with
the authority to review not only executive or administrative actions but also laws enacted by
Parliament and State Legislatures. This power flows from Articles 226, 32, and 136 of the
Constitution, which collectively empower constitutional courts to protect rights and enforce
constitutional limitations. However, the Court emphasized that judicial review of legislative action
operates within narrower parameters when compared to the review of administrative decisions.
While courts undoubtedly possess the power to invalidate legislation, such power is exercised only
on well-defined and limited grounds. Primary legislation may be struck down if it transgresses the
constitutional distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States, or if it violates
fundamental rights or other express provisions of the Constitution. The judiciary’s role as the final
interpreter of the Constitution places it in the position of ultimate arbiter on questions concerning
the existence, scope, and violation of rights.
This authority is firmly rooted in Article 13(2) of the Constitution, which prohibits the State from
enacting any law that abridges or takes away the fundamental rights guaranteed under Part III.
Any law made in contravention of this mandate is rendered void to the extent of such
inconsistency. Judicial review, therefore, serves as the constitutional mechanism through which
this prohibition is enforced, ensuring the continued vitality of fundamental rights and
constitutional supremacy.
Source: Excerpt from the case of Justice K.S.Puttaswamy (Retd) vs Union of India 2018

landmark judgment on 8 April 2025, addressing the constitutional limits on the powers of a state

Governor lacks an unfettered veto or “pocket veto” over legislation duly adopted by the State
Assembly and emphasised that the Governor must act in accordance with constitutional
conventions and the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers. The Court observed that prolonged
withholding of assent or referral of bills for presidential consideration undermines democratic
mandates and federal principles. In that context, the bench-imposed timelines directing that
Governors decide on re-enacted bills within one month and on bills reserved for the President
within three months to prevent indefinite delays that can frustrate the legislative will of elected
representatives. Utilizing its powers under Article 142 of the Constitution in the exceptional facts

legislatures. www.lawpreptutorial.com

questions.stimulus:
XIII. The status of the Preamble has been one of the most debated subjects in Indian constitutional
jurisprudence, serving as the focal point for defining the relationship between the spirit and the
"letter" of the law. The Preamble to the Constitution of India records the aims and aspirations of
the people, yet its legal enforceability and its status as an integral part of the constitutional
document underwent a significant evolution through two landmark judicial pronouncements. The
first major confrontation with this issue occurred in In Re: Berubari Union (1960). The Supreme
Court was tasked with an advisory opinion regarding the transfer of certain territories to
Pakistan. During the proceedings, the role of the Preamble as a guide to legislative intent was
discussed. The Court acknowledged that the Preamble is a "key to open the mind of the makers"
and shows the general purposes for which they made the several provisions in the Constitution.
However, the Court explicitly held that the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution.
Consequently, it was viewed as a decorative introduction that lacked substantive power. The
Court reasoned that since it is not a part of the Constitution, it cannot be regarded as a source of
any substantive power or a limitation on the powers of the government.
This restrictive view remained the law of the land until it was directly challenged and overturned
in the historic case of Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973). A 13-judge Bench the
largest in the history of the Court re-examined the Preamble's status while determining the scope
of Parliament's amending power under Article 368. The Court observed that the history of the
drafting of the Constitution showed that the Preamble was not just an introduction but was
actually voted upon by the Constituent Assembly, unlike the preambles of many other world
constitutions. In a monumental shift, the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is a part of the
Constitution. Justice Sikri observed that the Preamble is of extreme importance and the
Constitution should be read and interpreted in the light of the grand and noble vision expressed in
it. More importantly, the Court held that the Preamble contains the Basic Structure of the
Constitution, which is beyond the amending power of Parliament. While the Preamble itself can be
amended (as it was in 1976), such amendments cannot destroy its fundamental pillars like
secularism, democracy, or socialism.

constitutiona-ideals-and-aspirations /?

access to protective measures such as air purifiers. The Supreme Court has since taken suo motu
cognisance of the controversy and is scheduled to hear the matter. The second decision highlighted

XV. Amid loud protests from the opposition, the Karnataka Legislative Assembly on December 18
passed the Karnataka Hate Speech and Hate Crimes (Prevention) Bill, 2025, in Belagavi. The
legislation prescribes imprisonment of one to seven years along with fines for hate crimes. For
repeat offences, imprisonment ranges from two to seven years with higher fines. The Bill covers
communication made in public through verbal, print, public, or electronic means.
While tabling the Bill, Home Minister G. Parameshwara cited a Supreme Court ruling delivered
on May 5 this year, which emphasised the need for firm action against communal hate. He noted
that hate speech had led to killings and inter-community violence, harming social harmony. The
legislation aims to protect constitutional values by addressing discrimination rooted in religion,
race, caste, gender, language, and other identities. According to Parameshwara, the objective is to
curb and prevent dissemination, publication, or promotion of hate speech that causes disharmony
or hatred against a person or group. The home minister explained that existing preventive
restrictions on provocative speech were insufficient. Alerts about potential inflammatory speech
could lead to temporary bans, but this was not a long-term solution. Therefore, a separate law was

required, as provocative speeches were often followed by violent incidents. The government is
authorised to direct the removal of hate speech material from media platforms. Hate crime under
the Bill is defined as communicating or promoting hate speech to cause disharmony, enmity, or ill-
will against individuals or groups.
The Bill makes hate speech a cognizable, non-bailable offence, and offenders can be tried by a
Judicial Magistrate First Class. For organisations, persons in charge at the time of the offence are
deemed liable.
The Congress government-initiated discussions on a hate speech law in June after a series of
communal killings in coastal Karnataka, beginning with the lynching of a Muslim man, Ashraf, in
April. Leader of the opposition R. Ashok opposed the Bill, tearing a copy in the assembly and
claiming it infringed on Article 19(1), which guarantees free expression. He argued that police
could misuse the law for political purposes, targeting journalists and opposition members. Ashok
suggested existing provisions in the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita were adequate. The debate
intensified after Urban Development Minister Byrathi Suresh made a remark directed at BJP
MLA Vedavyas Kamath, prompting the opposition to demand its removal from the official record.
Despite protests, Parameshwara appealed for support, and the speaker announced the Bill had
been approved through a voice vote before adjourning the House for lunch. BJP MLAs later stated
they were caught off guard by the passage without full debate. Minister for Law H.K. Patil
emphasised that the Bill had been passed and could not be discussed again. The Bill seeks to
address communal disharmony by making hate speech and hate crimes punishable under clear
statutory provisions, ensuring swift action against offenders and promoting social harmony in
Karnataka.
Source: The Wire dated Article 19» December 2025

questions.stimulus:
XVII. The recent nationwide strike by a vast cohort of gig workers has exposed the precariousness
embedded within India’s emerging labour framework for platform-mediated work. This unrest
unfolded immediately after the Labour Ministry released draft Rules to operationalise the revised
labour codes, highlighting a fundamental disjunction between regulatory intent and lived labour
realities. While these Rules formally acknowledge gig workers within the social security
architecture, they conspicuously exclude them from statutory protections relating to wages and
working conditions. By severing gig work from the traditional employment relationship for wage
determination, the framework relegates platforms to the limited obligation of making aggregate
contributions to a social security fund, leaving core worker grievances unresolved. The Code on
Wages, though ostensibly universal, exempts gig workers by categorising their labour as distinct
from employment, thereby permitting algorithmic rate reductions and opaque incentive
mechanisms to persist unchecked. Similarly, the Occupational Safety, Health and Working
Conditions Rules adopt a compliance-centric model predicated on employer reporting via the
Shram Suvidha Portal — an approach ill-suited to the dispersed, app-mediated nature of gig
labour. In effect, social security emerges as the sole substantive reform, yet even here, access
remains contingent and procedurally burdensome. Under the draft provisions, gig workers must
register on a designated portal, while aggregators are required to periodically upload engagement
data. Eligibility hinges on minimum thresholds of 90 days with a single platform or 120
cumulative days across platforms within a financial year. Although multiple engagements within
a single day may be counted multiplicatively, this technical accommodation fails to constrain
platform control over work allocation. More critically, such temporal thresholds risk penalising
workers engaged in unpaid care labour, suffering illness, maternity-related interruptions, or
facing demand volatility beyond their control.

Consequently, the draft Rules necessitate substantive redesign to ensure that social security is not
merely nominal but operationally meaningful. Threshold criteria must incorporate explicit
safeguards against involuntary work discontinuities and prevent lapses arising from transient
downturns. Furthermore, the framework must delineate the specific benefits available, prescribe
minimum entitlements supported by the Social Security Fund, and establish a transparent, time-
bound mechanism for claims, grievances, and appeals independent of platform discretion. Finally,
procedural transparency must be institutionalised. Aggregators should be mandated to furnish
workers with regular statements detailing tasks completed, hours logged, earnings accrued, and
deductions imposed, alongside a robust mechanism for contesting inaccuracies. Absent such
reforms, the proposed regime risks entrenching the very structural insecurity that precipitated
collective action among gig workers, rendering regulatory recognition hollow rather than
transformative.
